AI for Recruiters

Your best candidate for today's role is almost always someone already in your database — you just don't know which one, or that they're ready to move. We re-check your list against the live web, score every candidate against the actual requisition, and hand your desk a ranked list of who to call first and what to say.

The problem

You already paid to source them once

Staffing firms sit on thousands of candidates and work them like strangers.

Your database decays quietly

People change jobs, titles and cities. Your ATS doesn't find out. Every month the record you're calling from is a little further from the truth.

Outreach in the dark

Recruiters call and email without knowing who's actually open to move, who fits the brief, or who this role would genuinely win.

Desk time spent on the wrong people

Your scarcest resource is recruiter hours. Spent in list order instead of likelihood order, they drag down response and placement rates.

How we rank

One Win Score, three honest questions

Every candidate is scored on three axes and rolled into a single number — with a one-line reason attached to each, so a recruiter can disagree with it.

Fit — can they do it?

Skills, seniority and experience against the requisition, judged on their actual title and history. Clear over-qualification is penalised as heavily as under-qualification.

Pull — would they say yes?

The likely comp delta, a title or level bump, and whether the company is a step up in trajectory or brand. Comp reads stay deliberately approximate — a range, never a fake precise number.

Intent — are they ready to move?

Two axes: the person's own openness signals, and distress at their current employer. The employer signal is weighted below the person's, so it nudges the ranking rather than deciding it.

In depth

Privacy and synthetic data

These two decide how much of your data estate is usable at all — so they deserve more than a bullet.

PII & privacy

Know where it is, then control it

  • Discovery at scale. Find personal data across databases, documents, tickets and logs — including the copies nobody documented.
  • Classification. Know which kind of personal data it is, so the right handling rule follows automatically.
  • Masking, redaction, tokenization. Applied before data reaches a model, a vendor or a non-production environment.
  • Purpose-based access. The same field visible to the team that needs it and hidden from the one that doesn't.
  • Subject requests. Locate every instance of one person's data so access and deletion requests are answerable.
  • Privacy-preserving analysis. Answer the question without exposing the underlying records.
Synthetic data

Realistic data that isn't anyone's

  • Safe non-production. Test and development environments with no real customers sitting in them.
  • Rare events. Generate the fraud patterns and edge cases you have too few real examples of to learn from.
  • Balanced training sets. Correct skew without throwing away the data you already have.
  • Shareable datasets. Work with vendors, partners and researchers without moving real records.
  • Stress testing. The awkward inputs that break systems, generated on demand instead of discovered in production.
  • Honest caveat. Synthetic data is a tool, not a loophole — we validate utility and re-identification risk before anyone relies on it.
What changes

The shifts worth planning for

  • The 80% becomes usable. Most of what an organization knows has always been unstructured and therefore invisible to analysis. That constraint is gone.
  • Governance becomes enforcement. Classification and access stop being a policy document and become something the system applies on every request.
  • Privacy stops being the blocker. Automated PII handling and synthetic data mean "we can't use that data" turns into "we can use a safe version of it".
  • Questions stop queuing. Natural-language access to governed data means analysis no longer waits behind a reporting backlog.
  • Data work moves up. Less pipeline babysitting and manual tagging, more deciding what the business should actually measure.

Optimized AI: Why the Leanest Model Wins

The instinct is to point the biggest model at everything. It's also how AI budgets die. Our position — and the way the whole platform is built — is that ROI comes from matching each task to the leanest model that does it well.

The idea

Most work isn't hard — it's just constant

Inside any workflow, the tasks split sharply: a large share is routine and templated, a smaller share needs real reasoning, and only a sliver is genuinely difficult. Paying frontier-model prices for the routine share is where AI spend quietly leaks.

Right-size every task

Each job runs on the smallest model that clears the quality bar for it — measured, not assumed.

Route by difficulty

Hard cases escalate to stronger models automatically; easy ones never touch them.

Reuse what repeats

Repeated context is cached instead of re-paid — the same instructions shouldn't cost full price twice.

Three tiers, one rule: earn the escalation

01

Fast

The default. Short, templated, high-volume work — classification, extraction, confirmations, voice turns. Speed and unit cost matter most here, and quality holds.

Smart

Promoted deliberately, task by task: research, contracts, reports, policy work — anywhere reasoning quality visibly changes the output.

03

Power

Reserved for the rare, genuinely hard problems. If nothing on your workload needs it, you shouldn't be paying for it — most months, nothing does.

title: Voice AI in Production: Field Notes
html:
Research

Voice AI in Production: Field Notes

Our voice agents answer real phones for real businesses every day — restaurants, clinics, salons, hospitality. These are the things production teaches you that a demo never will.

Hear one on your number See the Voice Agents product
What production teaches

The demo is the easy part

Getting a voice agent to sound impressive for two minutes is easy. Getting it to take the 400th call of the week without embarrassing you is the actual job.

The first seconds decide

Callers judge the agent before it finishes its first sentence. Answer fast, speak naturally, get to the point.

Turn-taking beats vocabulary

Handling interruptions, pauses and corrections gracefully matters more than knowing every word.

Escalation is a feature

The best agents know exactly when to stop being an agent — and hand off with the story so far.

Field notes

Six lessons from live calls

  • Hold one language unless asked. Mishearing a word must never flip the conversation into another language mid-call — understand many, answer consistently in one.
  • Confirm outside the call. An order or booking isn't done until the SMS or email lands. The confirmation is what customers trust, not the conversation.
  • Let people finish — then don't restart. Barge-ins, second thoughts and "actually, make that two" are the normal case, not the edge case.
  • End cleanly. Clipping the goodbye undoes a perfect call. The last seconds carry more weight than they should — respect them.
  • Every call becomes a record. Transcripts, outcomes and follow-ups logged automatically — that audit trail is what turns "seems fine" into measured trust.
  • Watch the calls you used to miss. The clearest early win isn't handled volume — it's the evening and weekend calls that used to ring out and now become orders.

Containment, clean hand-offs and recovered missed calls — read the transcripts weekly, not the vibes.
